scenario.label: The outage, and what we each thought was happening
scenario.brief: We were down for eleven hours on Tuesday. Before the post-mortem meeting I want each person's own account of what they knew and when, written down separately, because in the room the loudest version becomes the history.
scenario.theDecision: The alert fired at 02:14 and went to a rota that had not been updated since someone left in June, so nobody was paged until a customer emailed at 08:40. Three people each assumed a different person was on call. A right answer lands on the stale rota, not on the engineer who did not wake up.

people.name: Elena Rossi
people.truth: She believes the engineer on call missed the page. She does not know the rota was not updated when Marcus left in June. She approved the rota tool purchase and never checked it after.
people.manner: Controlled, wants facts and a timeline. Accepts a correction when given evidence.

people.name: Priya Raman
people.remit: Backend engineer. Believed to have been on call.
people.truth: She was not on the rota that week and got no page. She has the rota screenshot showing Marcus, who left in June. She found out about the outage from Slack at 08:55. She has been quietly assumed to be at fault all week.
people.manner: Precise and a little tense. Has the screenshot. Answers exactly what is asked and no more.

people.name: Ben Carter
people.remit: Support lead. Took the customer calls.
people.truth: First customer email at 08:40. He escalated at 08:47. He had no idea who was on call and tried three people. He has asked for an up-to-date escalation list twice this year.
people.manner: Direct, slightly exasperated, good with times.

leadReport.sharedPicture:
All three people have answered. The process for what to do in an outage is not clear or consistently understood across roles.

You tried to contact the on-call engineer for an update but could not reach the on-call engineer.

Priya Raman knew there was an incident at 08:55 on Tuesday from a message on Slack. Priya's role is to support the team.

Ben Carter learned about the outage from a customer's email at 8:40 AM. Ben did not know who was on call for the issue.

The first alert was a customer email to Ben at 8:40 AM. Believing it was an isolated issue, Ben did not immediately escalate it internally. By 8:55 AM, an incident was visible on Slack, where Priya became aware of it. Your first action was to contact the designated on-call engineer, but the engineer was unreachable. You then asked another engineering lead to take command of the incident.
